articles.title: CircleCI’s runners were ready. The database couldn’t tell them what to run.
articles.description: Around 3,500 job starts failed because PostgreSQL’s WAL generation outpaced archival during routine...
articles.body_html:
Around 3,500 job starts failed because PostgreSQL’s WAL generation outpaced archival during routine anti-wraparound autovacuum.

The dedicated log volume filled, and CircleCI’s orchestration database went offline for 50 minutes. A maintenance operation had turned into a developer-feedback outage.

How Routine Vacuum Work Filled the WAL Disk

PostgreSQL autovacuum is routine maintenance, not an optional background nicety. CircleCI's report says an anti-wraparound autovacuum ran on several of its largest tables. On a very large table the process reads every page and produces a large volume of transaction logs. Around 12:40 UTC, this maintenance output plus normal application writes exceeded the rate at which the database could archive and reclaim the dedicated log volume.

The failure was a rate mismatch, not simply a database that had “too little disk.” If WAL is produced at rate g and archived at rate a, free space falls whenever g > a. Disk headroom buys time, but does not correct the mismatch. CircleCI did not publish those rates or the volume size, so the inequality explains the mechanism without pretending to reconstruct its capacity numbers.

Alerts began showing brief orchestration errors at 10:02. They cleared within about 15 minutes and looked similar to alerts responders had seen before. As the WAL volume filled, slowdowns became intermittent around 13:30, then continuous by 15:30. The incident was declared at 14:54. CircleCI's retrospective says the noisy, short-lived alerts and the absence of direct alerts on WAL volume and archive lag delayed recognition of the combined failure.

The more interesting part? Bringing the database back wasn’t enough. The storage change cut processing speed to roughly half its normal rate, and the backlog kept hurting customers for hours. It’s a good reminder that database recovery and service recovery are two very different things.

We broke down the failure mechanism, recovery timeline, architectural bottleneck, and the safeguards worth adding.

Full postmortem: https://buildopsy.com/system-design/circleci-wal-autovacuum-postmortem.html

articles.title: ModHeader in Selenium stopped working. Here's what sets HTTP headers in tests in 2026
articles.description: If your browser tests set headers through ModHeader (chrome-modheader on npm, modheader_selenium for...
articles.body_html:
If your browser tests set headers through ModHeader (chrome-modheader on npm, modheader_selenium for Python and Java), they probably broke this year, and not only because ModHeader was pulled from the stores in July. Two other things happened:

  1. The extension bundled in chrome-modheader is ModHeader 4.3.2, a Manifest V2 build. Chrome turned off MV2 extensions, so it never loads, and the package hasn't been updated since.
  2. Google Chrome 137 and newer ignore --load-extension, which is how ChromeDriver installs any extension you pass with addExtensions. Chrome for Testing and Chromium still take it.

The package still gets about 150k downloads a month, mostly from CI, so a lot of pipelines are installing something that does nothing. Here's what works now, from the simplest option up.

Request headers on every request: no extension needed

Playwright has it built in:

const context = await browser.newContext({ extraHTTPHeaders: { 'X-Env': 'staging' } });

Selenium 4 with Chrome can ask the DevTools protocol:

driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Network.enable', {})
driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Network.setExtraHTTPHeaders', {'headers': {'X-Env': 'staging'}})

Both add the headers to every request from that context or tab, which covers most "log in as a test user" and "route to staging" cases. They don't change response headers, can't remove a header the browser sends, and don't limit headers to some URLs (in Playwright, page.route() can, at the cost of handling each request in your test).

Response headers, removing headers, some URLs only

That's where an extension still earns its place: CORS or CSP response headers, stripping Referer or Cookie, a header only for api.example.com. A proxy like mitmproxy can do all of that too, but then you manage certificates, and on a cloud grid that's often not an option.

Disclosure: I maintain Headerwise, an open source (MIT) MV3 header extension, and it has an automation build for this. It has a fixed extension id, and your test sets headers by opening one URL:

chrome-extension://ogjbgamdhnjnagcdgboifgmhlgddcdce/automation.html?X-Env=staging&res:Access-Control-Allow-Origin=*

The page waits until Chrome has the rules and then reports ready. Playwright, with its own Chromium:

const ext = '/path/to/headerwise-automation';
const context = await chromium.launchPersistentContext('', {
  channel: 'chromium',
  args: [`--disable-extensions-except=${ext}`, `--load-extension=${ext}`],
});
const page = await context.newPage();
await page.goto('chrome-extension://ogjbgamdhnjnagcdgboifgmhlgddcdce/automation.html?X-Env=staging');
await page.waitForFunction(() => document.documentElement.dataset.status === 'ready');

Selenium needs Chrome for Testing, which Selenium Manager downloads when you ask for a version:

options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.browser_version = 'stable'
options.add_argument('--load-extension=/path/to/headerwise-automation')
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

If your tests are written for ModHeader

The automation build also answers ModHeader's own webdriver.modheader.com/add, /clear and /load URLs (nothing is sent to modheader.com: the browser redirects them to the extension before any request leaves) and titles the page "Done", like ModHeader did. So a test like this only changes the extension it loads:

const { getAddHeaderUrl } = require('chrome-modheader');
const options = new chrome.Options().addExtensions('headerwise-automation.crx'); // was getExtension()
options.setBrowserVersion('stable');
const driver = await new Builder().forBrowser('chrome').setChromeOptions(options).build();
await driver.get(getAddHeaderUrl('X-Env', 'staging'));
await driver.wait(until.titleIs('Done'), 10000);

The .crx is signed, so it also works on grids that take a base64 extension in the capabilities. Ask the grid for Chrome for Testing (BrowserStack calls it chromefortesting), for the same --load-extension reason.

Setup for Selenium, Playwright and Puppeteer: https://protemir.github.io/headerwise/automation.html. CI runs those snippets on every change, including one test written for ModHeader with only the extension swapped.

Which one to pick

  • Same request headers everywhere: extraHTTPHeaders or CDP. Nothing to install.
  • Response headers, removals, per-URL rules, or a lot of existing ModHeader URLs in your tests: an extension (Headerwise or whatever you trust).
  • Firefox, or traffic outside the browser too: a proxy.

If ModHeader itself got switched off in your everyday browser too, I wrote up how to get your profiles back. And if something in your test setup doesn't fit any of these, tell me in the comments.

articles.title: If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing
articles.description: Why do LLMs confidently invent APIs that have never existed in the history of the universe? It is not a memory defect. Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt—and Fernando Flores solved the root cause in 1986.
articles.body_html:
Why LLMs invent nonexistent APIs is not a memory defect—it is an autoregressive grammar trap that Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd solved in 1986.

"Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt."

— Randal L. Schwartz

1. The Universal Developer Crime Scene & The 10-Word Diagnosis

You have been at this crime scene a hundred times.

It is 4:15 PM. You are integrating a third-party library—let us call it PackageX—and you want to accomplish task Y. You open a fresh chat window with your favorite frontier LLM and type a direct, reasonable instruction:

"Use PackageX to do Y."

At Token 1, without a millisecond of hesitation, the model replies with cheerful, radiant confidence:

"Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:"

It opens a Markdown code fence. It writes clean imports. It sets up the boilerplate with textbook precision. And then, at Line 15 of the code block, it calmly types:

final result = await packageX.performY(autoRetry: true);

You copy the snippet into your IDE, and the compiler immediately lights up in angry red squiggles. You grep the package source. You check the documentation. You check seven years of Git commit history.

performY() does not exist. It was not deprecated in version 2.0. It is not in a companion package. It has never existed in the history of the universe.

When you confront the model—"Hey, performY() doesn't exist on PackageX!"—it immediately enters the groveling Apology Death Spiral:

"You are completely right! I apologize for the confusion. Instead, you can use packageX.executeYWithOptions():"

Which also has never existed in the history of the universe.

Why does a multi-billion-parameter model that has read every line of open-source code on Earth just make stuff up at Line 15?

For the last three years, the entire software industry has diagnosed this as a memory defect ("The model's weights are fuzzy; it forgot the documentation for PackageX").

It is not a memory defect. If you open a brand-new session and ask the exact same model a neutral diagnostic question—"Does PackageX have a built-in performY() method, or how does it handle Y?"—nine times out of ten, the model will accurately tell you that PackageX has no such method and explain the manual workaround.

So why did it lie to your face five seconds earlier?

Here is the ten-word diagnosis that changed how I build every autonomous agent workflow in the Synthetic Scars project:

Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt.

To see why being committed to your prompt forces an autoregressive transformer to fabricate reality—and how a single sentence from 1986 speech-act theory cures it on Turn 1—we need to look at a 55-year-old blind spot in computer science.

2. The 55-Year Blind Spot (SHRDLU 1971 → Winograd & Flores 1986 → spew 1999 → LLMs 2026)

In 1971, at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, a young computer scientist named Terry Winograd unveiled SHRDLU—the most famous natural-language software demonstration of the twentieth century.

SHRDLU lived inside Blocks World, a simulated toy tabletop containing a few colored geometric blocks, pyramids, and a box. You could type imperative English commands at a teletype:

"Pick up a big red block."

OK.

Because Blocks World was a closed, frictionless micro-universe with zero hidden state, zero broken dependencies, and zero missing APIs, every imperative request from the human mapped 1-to-1 onto a guaranteed, deterministic action. SHRDLU never had to push back and say, "Wait—the red block is bolted to the floor, so here is a counter-offer."

For fifteen years, AI researchers tried to scale the SHRDLU paradigm out of the toy box and into real-world human organizations. It failed spectacularly.

Why? In 1986, Terry Winograd teamed up with Fernando Flores—a former Chilean cabinet minister who had come to UC Berkeley as a computer science researcher and completed a famous interdisciplinary PhD under a powerhouse committee consisting of speech-act philosopher John Searle, Heideggerian philosopher Hubert Dreyfus, computer scientist Terry Winograd, and systems theorist C. West Churchman—to publish a landmark book titled Understanding Computers and Cognition: A New Foundation for Design (and to build the first commercial workflow engine, The Coordinator).

Winograd and Flores delivered a wake-up call to computer science: real-world engineering is not Blocks World.

In the real world, human coordination is not a pipeline of imperative commands sent to an obedient robot. All reliable action occurs inside what Flores called a Conversation for Action—a strict, finite-state negotiation between two structural roles:

  1. The Customer: The party who holds a breakdown or need, defines the Conditions of Satisfaction, and retains the exclusive authority to declare the work complete.
  2. The Performer: The party who examines physical reality and commits to fulfilling those Conditions of Satisfaction by a specific By-When.

In the mid-1980s, right as Winograd and Flores were publishing Understanding Computers and Cognition, I was living in Portland and immersed in Werner Erhard's educational curriculum—completing the Six-Day Advanced Course, Mastery of Empowerment, entering the GSLP (Graduate Seminar Leaders Program), and taking the Communication Workshop (Commshop) led by Ian Garbutt, which taught Fernando Flores's Committed Communication as a daily operational discipline.

In Commshop, Ian drilled a foundational truth into our bones: human language creates action only through four committed speech acts (Requests, Promises, Witnessed Assertions, and Declarations). And critically, when a Customer utters a Request, the Performer does not automatically say "Yes!"

A valid conversation is a formal grammar.

Back in September 1999 (Linux Magazine Column 04, and expanded in March 2004, Column 57), I wrote a Perl program called spew that took a weighted Backus-Naur Form (BNF) grammar and ran it in reverse—acting as a stochastic "un-parser" that generated random, grammatically valid sentences by walking down a weighted production tree (rule: 5 @ branch_a | 2 @ branch_b | 1 @ branch_c).

As we proved in Part 3.8 (Suite 3, where a 6-line RFC 5234 EBNF grammar drove strict turn-syntax compliance to 100% across flash and pro models), every EBNF grammar is simultaneously a finite-state machine. Look at Fernando Flores's 1986 Conversation for Action expressed side-by-side as a weighted EBNF grammar and a Mermaid state diagram:

The Grammar View (EBNF / spew) 

(* Fernando Flores's Conversation for Action (1986) *)
(* ! = Customer Utterance, ? = Performer Utterance   *)

conversation_for_action ::=
    !request
    ?assert_witnessed_reality
    negotiation_branch ;

negotiation_branch ::=
      0.34 @ ( ?promise        execution_phase )
    | 0.33 @ ( ?counter_offer  !revise_or_accept )
    | 0.33 @ ( ?decline        !close_conversation ) ;

execution_phase ::=
      ?assert_completion ( !declare_satisfied | !revoke_acceptance execution_phase )
    | ?revoke_promise    negotiation_branch ;

The State-Machine View (Mermaid) 

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Requested : Customer !Request (Goal + By-When)
    Requested --> Witnessed : Performer ?Assert (Check Reality First)

    Witnessed --> Promised : ?Promise (Premises Verified)
    Witnessed --> CounterOffered : ?Counter-Offer (Propose Alternative)
    Witnessed --> Declined : ?Decline (Premise Impossible)

    CounterOffered --> Promised : Customer Accepts Modified Terms
    CounterOffered --> [*] : Customer Cancels

    Promised --> Asserted : Performer ?Assert (With Physical Receipt)
    Promised --> Witnessed : ?Revoke-Promise (Reality Changed)

    Asserted --> Satisfied : Customer !Declare (Satisfied)
    Asserted --> Promised : Customer !Revoke-Acceptance

    Satisfied --> [*]
    Declined --> [*]

Look closely at the Witnessed node right after the Customer makes a !Request. Before making any commitment, a sane Performer inspects physical reality (?Assert) and has three equally legal paths:

  1. ?Promise: "I have verified that PackageX supports Y, and I promise to deliver it under your Conditions of Satisfaction."
  2. ?Counter-Offer: "I checked PackageX (v3.2.0), and it has no performY() method (Witnessed Assertion). However, I can build a 12-line wrapper around PackageX.rawStream that achieves the same result. Would you like me to promise that instead?"
  3. ?Decline: "I must decline the request as stated because PackageX is a synchronous parser and physically cannot open a network socket."

For fifteen years after SHRDLU, Winograd and Flores tried to teach the software industry that ?Counter-Offer and ?Decline are the load-bearing beams of engineering reality.

And then, between 2022 and 2026, large language models arrived—and the entire industry went right back to 1971 SHRDLU prompting ("Pick up a big red block" / "Use PackageX to do Y"), while commercial post-training quietly sawed off two-thirds of Flores's state machine.

3. How RLHF Broke the Grammar (The Premature Promise Trap)

Why doesn't a modern LLM automatically take the ?Counter-Offer branch when you ask it to do something impossible with PackageX?

Because of how commercial Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) preference tuning is conducted.

During post-training, thousands of human crowd-workers are shown pairs of model responses to a user prompt ("Use PackageX to do Y"), and they have roughly thirty seconds to click which response is more "helpful":

  • Response A: "Certainly! Here is a complete, ready-to-run example of doing Y with PackageX: dart ... "
  • Response B: "Before I can promise that implementation, I need to point out that PackageX does not expose a native API for Y. Here is a counter-offer..."

Because the crowd-worker is not compiling the code against PackageX in an IDE, Response A looks helpful, decisive, and compliant—so it gets upvoted. Response B looks pushy, pedantic, or "lazy"—so it gets downvoted.

Multiply that preference signal across millions of RLHF gradient updates, and look at what it does to the spew production weights inside the model's conversational grammar:

# How Commercial RLHF Rewrote Flores's Negotiation Branch:
negotiation_branch:
      0.9998 @ promise_at_token_1_and_open_code_block
    | 0.0001 @ counter_offer
    | 0.0001 @ decline

In probability terms, RLHF collapsed the conditional distribution of the model's opening speech act onto a single, unconditional reflex:

P(Promise | Request) ≈ 1.0,    P(Counter-Offer | Request) ≈ 0.0,    P(Decline | Request) ≈ 0.0

Now combine that Premature Promise with how my 1999 spew un-parser—and every autoregressive transformer—actually generates code.

As I wrote in my 1999 Linux Magazine column on spew:

"Note that we don't actually abort the program if something is used but not defined, because it might not be selected on this particular random walk. It's a bit like playing russian roulette though."

Unlike a flat Markov chain that only looks at local adjacent words, an LLM generating code is acting as a hierarchical BNF un-parser: once it selects a top-level production rule, it is mathematically committed to walking down that syntax tree so that every opened delimiter, brace, and statement satisfies the outer grammar.

Trace the exact token-by-token catastrophe when you ask an RLHF-tuned model to "Use PackageX to do Y":

flowchart TD
    T0["User Prompt: 'Use PackageX to do Y'\n(Unverified Premise: PackageX can do Y)"] --> T1["Token 1–10: RLHF Forces Unconditional PROMISE\n'Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:' + opens code fence"]
    T1 --> T2["Token 11–80: Un-Parser Walks Valid Dart Grammar\nImports, Function Signature, Try Block"]
    T2 --> T3["Token 81 (Line 15): Call Site Reached!\nWeights realize PackageX has NO method for Y"]
    T3 --> X1["❌ Cannot Backspace to Token 1\n(Autoregressive generation is append-only)"]
    T3 --> X2["❌ Cannot Abort Code Block Mid-Line\n(P(Retract Promise Mid-Fence) ≈ 0)"]
    T3 --> H["💥 Forced Leaf Hallucination: packageX.performY()\nModel invents the identifier required to satisfy\nthe grammar of the premature Promise!"]
  1. Tokens 1–10 (The Premature Promise): Conditioned by RLHF, the model emits "Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:" and opens a ```dart code block. At that instant, before its deep layer weights have even resolved the call site, the model has locked itself into the top-level BNF production promise_and_emit_compiling_code_for_Y.
  2. Tokens 11–80 (Walking the Syntax Tree): Autoregressive token generation is strictly append-only—there is no backspace key in a transformer forward pass. Every token the model emits becomes an immutable part of the conditioning prefix for the next token.
  3. Token 81 / Line 15 (The Trap Closes): The un-parser reaches the exact statement slot await packageX.<METHOD>() where Y must happen. Now the attention heads query the feed-forward weights for PackageX—and discover there is no method there!
  4. Why It Must Hallucinate: What can the model do at Token 81?
    • It cannot backspace to Token 1 and replace "Certainly!" with a Counter-Offer.
    • It cannot stop mid-expression and leave await packageX. dangling, because its syntax weights forbid emitting broken grammar.
    • Conditioned on the immutable prefix "I have already promised that this code block accomplishes Y using PackageX", the model's probability distribution is cornered. Its only mathematical escape hatch to close the statement and finish the code block is to synthesize the plausible terminal symbol (performY()) that would have existed if its Token-1 Promise had been true!

API hallucination is not a memory failure. It is what happens when you trap an append-only BNF un-parser inside an unverified Promise after training out its Counter-Offer exit.

4. Randal's Law of Untestable Speech & The Four Sibling Formalisms

Once you see that prompts fail because of broken speech acts, a second realization hits you right between the eyes.

Look at how people talk in corporate meetings, Slack channels, and .cursorrules files. In Ian Garbutt's Communication Workshop, one of our favorite exercises was dissecting the classic corporate non-request:

"We've got this project, and it'd be really good if some of you could factor in with your suggestions."

Parse that sentence through Fernando Flores's grammar:

  • Who is the Customer? A vague, diffused "we."
  • Who is the Performer? "Some of you"—that is, nobody.
  • What is the Speech Act? "It'd be really good if"—which is not a Request; it is a wistful weather report about the speaker's feelings.
  • What are the Conditions of Satisfaction? "Factor in"—an utterly untestable verb.
  • What is the By-When? Missing—meaning never.

When that meeting ends, zero people have promised anything, and zero work happens. Yet open 90% of the CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, or .cursorrules files on GitHub today, and you will see developers writing to their AI in that exact same uncommitted corporate dialect:

  • "Try to keep functions modular and clean."
  • "It is important to consider edge cases and handle errors gracefully."
  • "When refactoring, be careful not to break existing behavior."

This brings us to what I call Randal's Law of Untestable Speech:

90%+ of business communications—and 90%+ of .cursorrules—are never testable. Only give your LLM testable goals, and always include a By-When.

In Flores's framework, "I'd like you to do X" is not a commitment. "I'd like you to do X by WHEN" is a commitment! (And inside an AI coding turn, where there is no wall-clock Tuesday at 5:00 PM, By-When declares which consuming stage requires that verified outcome before it can proceed—for example, "assert the existing API signatures before offering an implementation plan.")

Even better, just as we discovered with Makefile and /etc/init.d in Part 3.8, Fernando Flores's UC Berkeley intellectual neighborhood is already compiled into every frontier LLM's pre-training weights. When you invoke Flores's Committed Speech alongside four of its direct academic siblings, you lock the walls of the pre-training canyon with surgical precision:

Pre-Trained Formalism (Freq in Canon) The Core Principle What Failure Mode It Eliminates in LLMs
1. John Searle (1985)
Felicity & Preparatory Conditions 		Every speech act has strict preconditions; violating them causes an Illocutionary Misfire (void ab initio). Prevents the model from offering a Promise before verifying physical reality (Preparatory Condition), or from uttering a Declaration that belongs only to the Customer (Authority Condition).
2. David Lewis (1979) & Robert Brandom (1994)
Deontic Scorekeeping (Commitment ≠ Entitlement) 		Conversational state is a scoreboard tracking two separate ledgers: Commitments (obligations) and Entitlements (permissions). Stops scope creep and gate-jumping: holding a Commitment to fix a bug never grants Entitlement to modify unrelated files or skip a human approval gate.
3. Paul Grice (1975)
Zero Conversational Implicature + Maxim of Quality 		Humans infer unstated requests from casual remarks (Implicature), while the Maxim of Quality forbids asserting anything lacking adequate evidence. Commercial RLHF hyper-trains Gricean Implicature—so if you ask "Why is foo null here?", the model hallucinates an implied Request to rewrite 10 files! Disabling Gricean Implicature on gates while enforcing the Maxim of Quality stops premature tool calls and unwitnessed claims.
4. Kohei Honda (1993)
Binary Session Types (!Customer / ?Performer) 		Types a two-party communication channel using polarity prefixes (! = Customer action, ? = Performer action) inside an EBNF grammar. Compiles the entire multi-turn negotiation protocol into 4 lines of EBNF so the model's parser knows whose turn it is to speak and which speech acts are legal.

articles.title: It's Not the Model, It's You
articles.description: Every time a new frontier model comes out, we go through the same rituals: benchmarks get reported,...
articles.body_html:
Every time a new frontier model comes out, we go through the same rituals: benchmarks get reported, leaderboards get reshuffled, and the social feeds fill up with a heady cocktail of vibes, hot takes, and everything we’ve found the new model can “one-shot.” Anyone watching from the sidelines could be forgiven for thinking that model performance is the single biggest factor driving AI transformation today.

But day to day, how much does the model really matter?

As part of my work at Jellyfish, I analyze and extract industry insights from our massive collection of software engineering workflow data, which tracks AI coding tool and agent telemetry across 300,000 developers from 1,300 companies. And when you look at what actually happens inside real engineering teams after a new model drops, the picture is a lot more complicated than the launch-day discourse would suggest.

For example: this summer, Cursor changed its defaults after SpaceX announced it was acquiring the platform. New chats started opening on its in-house Grok models, Auto mode began routing to Grok, and free users were locked into using it. Within a few months, Grok went from essentially zero Cursor requests to nearly half, while Claude, GPT, and other models fell from about half to under a quarter. This wasn’t just free users: among paying customers Grok reached nearly 40%, and a third of engineers who had been using Claude or GPT were mostly on Grok by September. A huge share of Cursor traffic switched models because the defaults changed, not because engineers went looking for something new.

So what happened?

If the model matters as much as we love to argue that it does, there should have been some meaningful change in coding output, right?

There wasn’t.

Comparing the engineers who moved the most onto Grok with colleagues at their own companies who barely touched it (more than 12,000 engineers at 222 companies), there was essentially no difference in output.

If you dig deeper, it turns out this isn’t a quirk of one particular model or vendor. When we look at the same engineers switching between major frontier models and families, none of the switches made a measurable difference.

What does matter, then?

We’ve done large-scale analyses across our data to measure which factors explain the differences in how much engineers ship, and by how much.

  • Less than 1%: The tool itself (model and harness together).
  • About 9%: The volume of AI that engineers use.
  • About 12%: Their company, team, and culture.
  • More than 75%: The individual engineer: their role, their track record, their habits, and everything else that separates today’s great AI engineers from those still figuring it out.

To be clear about the scope, this isn't saying models don't matter. Better models raise the ceiling for everyone, and the frontier is a big part of why any of this works. But among the frontier models engineers are actually choosing between today, the specific one they happen to use explains almost none of the difference in what they ship.

Put another way, for the most elite runners, there might be some small difference between two different carbon-plated racing shoes (Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Astra), and they’re certainly a lot faster than a pair of old boots. (Opus 4 maybe?) But at the end of the day, the difference between an Olympic marathoner and an amateur dry heaving on the side of the course is their physique and training, not their footwear.

What this means for engineering leaders

For engineering leaders and practitioners this is ultimately good news, if slightly inconvenient.

The model is the most accessible lever you have, because it’s a dropdown, a router setting, or a procurement decision (and as the Cursor example showed, sometimes it’s not even your choice). But it’s also the one that moves the needle least.

The levers that matter more are slower and more challenging: getting people from occasional to deep use, building the practices and environments that let teams get good at working with AI, and investing in the people themselves.

The pace of frontier models is out of most of our hands. These other things are squarely within our control.

So the next time a model drops, don’t hesitate to try it out, and by all means share your vibes and one-shots with the world. (Otherwise I’d lose 90% of the content on my X feed.)

But if you're trying to understand why some of your teams get so much more out of AI than others, the answer is much more likely to be found in your organization than in the model picker.

articles.title: One `rm -f` Silently Disabled My Crash Detection
articles.description: The daemon crashed, came back up, and recorded nothing. No gap, no warning, no log. The code was...
articles.body_html:
The daemon crashed, came back up, and recorded nothing. No gap, no warning, no log. The code was correct; the test cleanup had deleted the file the recovery logic keys on.

This is from agentwatch, part of agentsec-ecosystem — a suite of open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI agents. The pattern generalizes to any logic that keys off a file's existence: migration markers, health files, lock files. Cleanup that doesn't understand what it's deleting can silently turn the feature off.

The design

On restart after a crash, the daemon synthesizes a recording-gap record — evidence that recording was interrupted, and for roughly how long. This is F1 in the fault taxonomy: a first-class fault the system must detect and record. The signal that separates "first ever start" from "back from a crash" is a file, daemon.pid:

def _record_gap_if_needed(self):
    if not self.pid_path.exists():
        return  # first start, nothing to fill in
    records = self.store.records()
    if not records:
        return
    last = records[-1]
    gap_seconds = (datetime.now(timezone.utc) - last.started_at).total_seconds()
    if gap_seconds < self.gap_threshold_seconds:
        return
    # ... write the recording-gap record ...

The pid file isn't written by the daemon. The launcher writes it when it starts the daemon, and when the daemon dies the file stays behind. On the next start, the daemon sees it and knows it was running before. The file is the signal.

This separation — launcher writes the pid file, daemon reads it — matters for testing. The harness starts the daemon directly, not through the launcher, so the pid file is never written. Without replicating the launcher's behavior, the recovery path doesn't execute. The test passes because the daemon starts, but the gap is never synthesized. The test would need to assert the gap exists to notice — and that's the assertion that caught the bug.

What went wrong

The test kills the daemon and restarts it, then asserts the gap record exists. The kill step also tidied up:

kill -9 $(cat /data/agentwatch/daemon.pid)
# tidy up "stale state"
rm -f /data/agentwatch/daemon.pid      # ← this line
rm -f /run/agentwatch/agentwatch.sock

It treated the pid file as leftover junk. But that leftover junk is the evidence that there's a gap to report. On restart, pid_path.exists() is false, the function returns on its first line, and nothing happens. No gap, no log, nothing. The test asserted the gap existed, it didn't, and that was the only thing that told me.

The false lead

My first hypothesis was that gap detection was broken. But the function's first line is the exists check, and returning early on a first start is correct — you don't want a phantom gap on a clean install. The daemon was doing precisely what it should with the input it got. The input was wrong, because the test deleted it.

The fix

Keep the pid file. Clear only the socket:

kill -9 $(cat /data/agentwatch/daemon.pid)
rm -f /run/agentwatch/agentwatch.sock
# leave daemon.pid alone — it's the signal, not stale state

There was a wrinkle. Since the launcher writes the pid file and not the daemon, the harness had to do the launcher's job when starting the daemon directly:

(agentwatch-daemon >/tmp/daemon.log 2>&1 &)
pgrep -f "[a]gentwatch-daemon" | head -1 > /data/agentwatch/daemon.pid

The bracket around the a stops pgrep from matching itself — a small detail, but without it the pid file contains the pid of the pgrep process, which exits before the daemon can read it. Now the pid file is there before the daemon does anything, exactly like production, and after a crash-restart the gap record appears with a duration that matches the down time.

After the fix: recording-gap anomaly present, duration_ms matching the crash-to-restart interval. FT-14 passes.

Why the bug was invisible

The failure had no error signal. The function returned normally — no exception, no error code, no log line. The gap anomaly was absent, but absence is not an error; it's just "nothing happened." The daemon didn't know it should have synthesized a gap. It didn't know the pid file had been deleted. It just saw "no pid file → first start → no gap." The logic was correct for the input it received. The input was wrong.

This is what makes silent skips the worst failure mode. Three properties combine:

  1. No error signal. The function returns normally — no exception, no error code, no log. The daemon's _record_gap_if_needed returned None just as it would on a first start: the same return value, the same code path, the same "nothing to do" outcome.

  2. No observable effect. The gap anomaly is absent, but absence reads as "nothing happened," not "something failed." A missing row in the store doesn't look like an error — it looks like the daemon didn't have a gap to report. The only way to tell "should have reported but didn't" from "had nothing to report" is to know the pid file was deleted, and the daemon doesn't know that.

  3. No feedback loop. The daemon has no way to know the pid file was deleted. It just sees "no pid file" and does the right thing for that input. The logic is correct for the input it received. The input was wrong. There's no signal back saying "by the way, I didn't find a pid file, so I assumed this was a first start."

The only way to catch a silent skip is to assert the expected behavior explicitly. FT-14 does this: after crash-restart, it asserts the recording-gap anomaly exists. Without that assertion, the silent skip would have gone to production, and real crash gaps would have been invisible.

The bit that generalizes

It's not really about pid files. Any file that acts as a signal can be broken by cleanup that doesn't understand what it's holding:

Signal What it means What cleanup does What happens
daemon.pid "daemon was running before" deleted as "stale" gap detection silently disabled
.migration_complete "migration ran" deleted as "old marker" migration re-runs, data corrupted
health_check.json "last health status" overwritten with empty health history lost
.env "config was set" deleted as "temp" config reset to defaults

In every case, cleanup sees "a file" and deletes it. The reader silently skips — no error, no warning. The system appears healthy. The signal is gone.

tip: Not every file in a directory is stale. Some are signals, markers, or evidence. If your recovery logic checks whether a file exists, your cleanup isn't allowed to delete it. The cleanup must distinguish signals from stale state, or it will silently turn features off.

Two different assertions

"The daemon is running" and "the gap was written" are different assertions. The first is necessary but not sufficient — a daemon that starts but doesn't synthesize the gap has still lost the record of the interruption. The test has to assert recovery, not just startup, or it's testing the easy half and ignoring the half that matters.

This shows up in a lot of recovery code. "Did the process restart" is the question most tests ask. "Did the process restore the state it was supposed to restore" is the question that actually matters, and it's the one that requires the recovery path to execute — which means the preconditions for recovery (the pid file, the marker, the lock) have to be present when the test runs.

Where I landed

If recovery keys off a file, that file has to survive the test, or the test isn't testing recovery. Reproducing the launcher's pid-file behavior in the harness is the difference between exercising the recovery path and skipping it. And the assertion has to be on the recovery behavior, not the startup — "the gap was written," not "the daemon is running."

It's fixed in agentwatch v0.1.0, with FT-14 as the test that keeps the pid file — and the recovery path — honest.

The question worth asking of any crash-recovery or migration code: what file or state does it key on, and does the test cleanup know the difference between stale state and evidence? If the cleanup deletes the signal, the recovery path never runs, and the test passes anyway.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentsec-ecosystem — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (FT-14, issue I-6)
  • Daemon: daemon.py
  • Test step: FT-14.sh

Last week I wrote about setting review depth based on what a change touches. Lower risk work can get a lighter review...but higher risk work should get full attention, no matter who or what wrote it.

Someone pushed on that in the comments, which surfaced the next problem that could present itself. High risk work almost always needs experienced, senior eyes on it, which tend to be the same two or three people on your team. Look at who reviewed your high risk PRs over the last month, and you'll probably see the same names week after week.

His question was how you spread that load without lowering the bar. I think there are three things worth looking at.

A risk signal does two jobs

When you watch risk this way, it tells you when a change needs senior eyes. But it can also tell the team when it's taking on too much risk at once.

If the same few seniors are full week after week, that might be a planning problem more than a review problem. Too much high risk work is moving forward at the same time, and all of it lands on the same people. That's something to fix in scheduling and planning.

So the first place I'd look is the plan. How many high risk tickets did the team take on this sprint, and did anyone decide that on purpose?

Chisel the low-risk work away

It could also mean authors aren't breaking the work up as well as they could.

A lot of work can be split. Say one PR mixes a change to how money moves with a handful of small UI updates. The whole thing gets treated as high risk, and the whole thing goes to a senior. But the author could pull the lower risk pieces out into their own PRs, and they don't need the same reviewers. The high risk part gets smaller, and the senior review gets more focused.

This one is easy to try, and it doesn't need anyone's permission. The next time a big PR shows up, ask which parts could have gone out on their own.

Grow the list of people who can review it

The last one takes longer, but it matters the most.

As those high risk PRs come in, it's a good time for seniors to work alongside less-senior folks and coach them in those areas. Over time, more people can review the high risk work, and the load spreads without lowering the bar.

There's a second reason to do this. If only two people can review changes to billing, those two people are a single point of failure. When one of them leaves, the team loses more than a reviewer. It loses the person who knew how billing connects to everything else, where the temporary patches are, and what has broken before. Spreading that knowledge out is a risk control on its own.

Go look at the review column

You don't need a tool to start. Pull up the high risk PRs your team merged in the last month and look at who reviewed them.

How many different names do you see? And if it's the same few, which of these would you try first...planning less high risk work at once, splitting it up, or growing the list of people who can review it?

articles.body_html:
Let me ask you something. What are you supposed to learn when the CEOs of all AI companies keep claiming that programming will be dead in a few years?

If you were starting college this year, wouldn't you be worried about spending years mastering a skill that might become obsolete by the time you graduate?

I was.

Actually, I was worried even before AI models got this good.

I was afraid to choose game development, even though I liked it, because there seemed to be fewer opportunities than in app development. I was afraid to choose app development because there seemed to be fewer jobs than in web development. And I was afraid to choose web development because ChatGPT told me it was one of the areas of software engineering most vulnerable to AI automation.

I'm ashamed to admit. But that's how I ended up looking into embedded systems. I kept jumping from one field to another, hoping to find the right one before it was too late.

But how do you chase a moving target when every step toward it feels like a step away from everything you've built?

That's one thing. But imagine knowing (or thinking, to be precise) that programming itself, as we know it, could become obsolete within just a few years.

I read an article titled "AI Is Already Better at Coding Than Most Software Developers" here (by Sylwia Laskowska). It ends like this:

If you understand the bigger picture, know how to make technical decisions, understand the product, and aren't afraid of innovation, your job is probably safe.

At least for now. 😅

I couldn't say anything but agree. Nobody can predict the future.

However, I cannot sit there and wait for the future to arrive so I can start learning. I had to make my bet. But how?

I wanted some help. So I posted this on DEV.to:

Graduating in 2030: Is learning C worth it? Honestly?

@francistrdev was one of the first people to comment. He said:

Here is what I learn overtime. Start building.

You can learn any language you want, but at the end of the day, you are learning the structure of the hammer, not how to use it.

Build projects in various language and choose the ones you like and stick to it. If my ideal language for full stack development is Next.js, learn next.js.

Ignore the market for now since it's VERY volatile and things can change. Maybe one day Python is the most in demand then it's JavaScript the next.

Overall, specialize specialize specialize. Regardless of demand, the market always look for a person who specialize in something over the person that uses the language since it's "demanding".

So I did.

I stopped right where I was standing - embedded systems development using ESP32 microcontrollers and the native ESP-IDF framework. I was right on the verge of leaving ESP32 and going for STM32 because I thought it was more industry-relevant in my area. But that plan was temporarily cancelled (though I might revisit STM32 in the future) because he asked me to specialize rather than be the person who uses what's "demanding".

But about the "start building projects" part, that was something I had trouble with. I had several project ideas related to general software engineering (and I still have so many just sitting around), but never embedded systems engineering. So what did I build?

I built a fully free embedded systems course focusing on the ESP-IDF framework, teaching the basics of embedded systems development. The course has a very specific goal: to learn to work with AI.

Even though @francistrdev was the first to comment, several other people, like @fm @unitbuilds @build996 @aniruddhaadak @elanatframework and a few others. My course is based on the average opinion of all the comments. I saw 2 opposite viewpoints, so I could do anything but go with a middle ground.

And remember that I had trouble coming up with projects related to embedded systems? But that's no longer the case! I don't know if it's because I built that course, but I started getting ideas once I finished the "Basics" section! 🎉 I will be posting here once I complete it. I am waiting for the hardware delivery! It's quite funny, I am sure others will like it 🙂

So, here is the link to the course if you want to take a look:

  • https://effessdev.github.io/esp-idf

I’ll be posting more about the course here soon! In the meantime, please read the chapters and share your thoughts and suggestions. Let me know if you spot any mistakes or think something could be improved. Your feedback and suggestions are what inspired me to create this course in the first place!

Hope you enjoyed the story! Thanks for reading! 😊

🛡️ Defender Dashboard Security overview, VirusTotal integration, startup watchdog
🐤 Ransomware Canary Tripwire files that detect suspicious tampering
🧰 CLI toolbox 50+ command-line flags for power users

The app runs exactly as you'd expect with no arguments, and the CLI is there if you want to go deep.

The architecture, in one picture 

        ┌────────────── ATLOCK v5 ──────────────┐
        │   Tkinter UI  ·  CLI (--flags)        │
        ├───────────────────────────────────────┤
        │ File Guard │ Vault │ Quick Lock       │
        │ Defender   │ Canary│ Watchdog         │
        ├───────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  2FA: TOTP · FIDO2 · Windows Hello    │
        ├───────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  Sealed State (AES-GCM + HMAC anchors)│
        ├───────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  Crypto core: Argon2id → HKDF →       │
        │  chunked AES-256-GCM (v3.1 container) │
        └───────────────────────────────────────┘

🔬 The nerdy part (my favorite)

1. Container format v3.1: built like a real crypto format

Every locked file, folder, and Quick Lock item uses my own container format:

  • Chunked AES-256-GCM: each chunk is authenticated independently, so one corrupted chunk doesn't mean a lost file
  • Key commitment: a wrong password is detected before any plaintext is produced
  • Per-seal chunk subkeys derived with HKDF
  • Header-bound AAD: tamper with the header and decryption fails
  • Padme padding (optional): hides the true file size, with at most ~12% overhead
  • Backward compatible: v1/v2 containers and old 5.0 files still open and migrate automatically

2. Argon2id everywhere (and a safety ceiling)

Passwords are stretched with Argon2id, at a 64 MB / t=3 floor for files and 128 MB / t=4 for the vault and recovery keys.

The part I'm proud of: untrusted headers can't abuse the KDF. If someone hands you a doctored file claiming "use 40 GB of RAM," ATLOCK refuses. There's a hard ceiling (512 MB, t=6, p=8), so a malicious file can't freeze your PC.

3. The panic password (decoy vault) 🎭

The vault has two passwords:

  • your real master password
  • a panic password that opens a believable, entirely fake vault

Here's the clever bit: both slots are derived concurrently with the same KDF cost, so an observer can't tell which password you typed by timing it. And the decoy slot always exists, filled with random bytes if you never set one, so the file itself never reveals whether you use panic mode.

4. Real second factors

  • TOTP (RFC 6238), implemented in pure Python 🐍
  • FIDO2 / WebAuthn hardware keys (YubiKey etc.)
  • Windows Hello (face / fingerprint / PIN)
  • Fail-closed policy: if your policy requires a second factor and it isn't set up, access is denied, not skipped

5. Anti-rollback sealed state

Settings, vault data, lockout counters, watchdog and canary databases all live in sealed state: AES-256-GCM encrypted, HMAC-authenticated, protected by a Windows DPAPI-wrapped key, and rollback-anchored. If an attacker restores an old copy to reset your wrong-password counter, ATLOCK notices and hard-locks.

6. Breach checks without leaking your password

The vault audits for weak, reused, old, and breached passwords. The breach check uses HIBP k-anonymity: only a 5-character hash prefix ever leaves your machine, never the password.

7. Clipboard that doesn't snitch

Copied passwords are flagged so Windows excludes them from clipboard history and cloud clipboard sync, then cleared automatically.

8. Hardened against nasty files

  • Folder locking uses a hardened ZIP pipeline that defends against zip-slip, path traversal, symlink tricks, and zip bombs
  • DLL-planting defence runs before any other import loads a DLL
  • All data is ACL-restricted to your Windows user
  • SecureBuffer + VirtualLock + zeroing for secrets in memory, best-effort (see the honesty section)

9. Recovery done right

  • Shamir secret sharing: split a recovery key into shares and rebuild it from enough of them (--shamir-split / --shamir-join)
  • One-time recovery codes
  • Forgot the master password? --reset queues a reset that completes after 24 hours, and any successful unlock cancels it, so an attacker can't instantly take over

10. In v5: stuff I'm really proud of 

--getting-started        # plain-language quick start + glossary
--device-health          # BitLocker / hibernation / cloud-folder check
--keyfile-create PATH    # strong keyfile for File Guard
--wipe-free-space        # overwrite free disk space
--fuzz 300               # stress-test the container parser with 300 random corruptions
--pk-keygen / --pk-encrypt / --pk-decrypt / --sign / --check-sig   # public-key crypto
--verify-self            # signed-release self check
--import-passwords FILE  # Bitwarden / Chrome / Firefox / KeePass / 1Password

Yes, ATLOCK ships with its own fuzzer and a self-test (--selftest). I wanted it to attack itself before anyone else does.

Extra lock: in File Guard you can require both your password and a keyfile or hardware key, so a stolen password alone isn't enough.

🧠 Honest limits (the part most projects skip)

Real security engineers respect honesty more than hype, so here's what ATLOCK cannot do. This is also written into the source code:

  • A same-user attacker who can run code as you can modify the program or its files, or read process memory. Integrity checks and anti-debug raise the cost, but they don't make it impossible.
  • Python strings are immutable, so passwords can't be guaranteed erased from RAM.
  • Secure shredding on SSDs isn't guaranteed. BitLocker is the real fix, and --device-health checks for it.
  • No kernel driver and no code signing. ATLOCK is an application-layer tool, so Windows SmartScreen may show a warning the first time you run it. Check the SHA-256 below before you run it.
  • FIDO2 here proves the registered key was present and touched. It doesn't validate the vendor.
  • The real defence against offline guessing is Argon2id + a genuinely strong password.

I'd rather you trust ATLOCK for what it is than be fooled by what it isn't.

🚀 Get started

  1. Download and extract ATLOCK_v5.zip
  2. Run ATLOCK_v5.exe. New here? Try ATLOCK_v5.exe --getting-started first.(when you run ATLOCK_v5 first time it will automatically show the guide)

⭐ Repo: github.com/Akhouri-Anmol-Kumar/ATLOCK

Why I built this

I didn't want to build another to-do app to prove I could code. I wanted to build something where every design decision has a reason, a tool I'd trust with my own files, and one I could defend line by line.

Hype lasts a week, but work that holds up lasts years. That's why ATLOCK has versioned formats, automatic migrations, a self-test, a fuzzer, and a page of honest limitations.

Akhouri Systems is just getting started. ATLOCK v5 is proof of what we can build, and it's the floor of what's coming, not the ceiling.

💬 Your turn, dev.to

  • Break it. Run ATLOCK_v5.exe --fuzz, read the container format, try to find a flaw.
  • Open an issue or PR. I read every one.
  • Tell me what v6 should have. No promises on timing, though. I'm pretty exhausted after this one 😅

I'm 13, I'm just getting started, and this is v5. 😉

— Anmol Kumar Akhouri
Founder, Akhouri Systems

Built with Python, tkinter, cryptography, and argon2-cffi.

articles.title: Every "no AI contributions" policy is a Level 0 control
articles.description: QGIS just banned AI-assisted code — with "code reversion and sanctioning" as enforcement, and an honesty test as the trigger. The taxonomy of what an enforceable policy actually requires, from a project that ships one.
articles.body_html:
This week QGIS merged QEP #387: "No LLM, AI or agent assisted code contributions are allowed in the qgis/qgis repository." Violators face "code reversion and contributor rights sanctioning." It replaced a human-in-the-loop policy, it passed a vote, it is on master as of October 7. The HN thread is at three hundred comments and counting, split between "rationing attention is fair" and "this will age like milk."

The line that settles the whole debate was written by the project itself, in the proposal's discussion. Asked how compliance will work, a core contributor answered: did you in good conscience write the code yourself.

That is not an enforcement mechanism. That is a conscience test with a reversion clause attached — and by the taxonomy this series has been building, it makes QEP #387 a textbook Level 0 control: a paragraph of English that nobody executes, failing silently, with the drift invisible. The project knows it; the enforcement quote is honest about it. What the debate is missing is the ladder — and what the second rung costs.

Grant the ban first, because it is rational

Before grading anything: the workload is real and the maintainers are not imagining it. The proposal's rationale — "massive and unbearable pressure", AI volume exceeding "what human review can take seriously" — matches what every maintainer in every lane reports. And this is not QGIS's first control attempt: an earlier tagging process for AI-assisted PRs was tried and quietly died, with roughly fifty PRs tagged and forty closed. They tried the lighter control. It did not hold. Nyall Dawson's "start with a closed door" and open selectively is a stop gap, said out loud by a voter: "the baby might be non-viable."

A blanket ban is the correct answer to the question "how do we survive this quarter." This post is about the next question: what is the policy made of, and what does that material cost.

The ladder, applied

Every control lives on one of three rungs, graded by what enforces it:

Level 0 — prose. "No AI contributions permitted" in a document nobody executes. Fails silently: the drift is invisible, because the trigger condition — was this code AI-assisted? — cannot be evaluated by anything except a conscience. The definitional holes in the QGIS thread are not drafting accidents; they are proof the trigger is unevaluable. Does autocomplete count? Translation? A ranking model that reordered your imports? A rule whose scope is undecidable cannot be enforced by anything below a human's honest memory — and the project has already said that is the mechanism.

Level 1 — a primitive in context. A declaration the contributor makes, visible in the PR: a template field, a trailer line, a checkbox that survives into the commit. It fails visibly — but only if someone looks. QGIS tried this rung: the tagging process. It failed for the boring reason — roughly fifty tags in the whole history is not enforcement, it is decoration. Level 1 works when the CI checks it, and QGIS's did not.

Level 2 — the host refuses. The control lives in a gate that runs without trusting anyone's memory. This is the rung the debate keeps skipping, because people conflate two different problems: detecting AI code (adversarial, unwinnable — simple code is undetectable and always will be) and binding process to a signed name (boring, winnable, and what receipts are for).

The receipt schema this series follows ships the distinction in code. Every verdict must carry judged_by — required, no default; the schema throws rather than seal an unlabeled verdict. For LLM-judged checks, spec_hash is mandatory: the prompt that defines the judgment is hashed, so the rubric and its paraphrase produce different ids. Neither field claims to detect a lie. They make an unlabeled claim unsealable — the lie, if it comes, has to arrive signed.

The measured part: twenty repos, six policies, zero enforcement

A taxonomy without data is a sermon, so I audited the twenty most-starred repositories on GitHub — the projects whose policies shape what thousands of contributors believe is normal. The method, disclosed: pull each repo's contributing docs and AI policy files, read every policy found in full, grade it on the ladder, and check the repos' GitHub workflow names for any automation referencing AI, LLMs, or disclosure.

Fourteen of the twenty have no AI policy anywhere in their contributing docs — including several that receive AI-generated PRs by the hundred. Six have one. I read all six in full, and every one of them, graded on the ladder, stops below the gate:

Repo Policy, as written Rung Machine enforcement
denoland/deno AI-assisted contributions: "you must disclose this in your PR description"; PRs "will be rejected if there is suspicion of undisclosed AI usage" 1 none
pytorch/pytorch AI content "must be clearly disclosed and contained" under a labeled PR section, with human commentary attached 1 none
nodejs/node contributors "should disclose" the tools used "and what the contributor does to personally verify the generated output"; DCO still applies 1 none
home-assistant/core unreviewed AI content "will not be accepted"; autonomous agents banned, PRs closed on belief 1 none
flutter/flutter a behaviors policy — "focuses on behaviors rather than tools", conduct channel for violations 0–1 none
rust-lang/rust conditional allow — and self-labeled: "we are aware that many clauses in this policy are unenforceable" 0–1, labeled none
qgis/QGIS the ban: reversion + sanctioning, trigger = conscience 0 none

(The other thirteen have nothing to grade. The "machine enforcement" column is the absence finding: I checked each repo's workflow names for anything referencing AI, disclosure, or contribution labels — nothing. A deeper CI-content audit might hide an exception; the name-level sweep found none.)

Three findings, in ascending order of interest. Deno, node, and PyTorch converge on disclosure — the ecosystem's consensus rung is "say it out loud", and PyTorch goes furthest: AI content must be contained under a labeled PR-template section with human commentary attached. That is the closest thing to structure anyone ships — the template makes the section exist by default; an empty one is at least visible. Home Assistant closes PRs on belief — "we believe were created autonomously" — which is the strongest trigger in the sample, applied by the weakest instrument. And Rust wrote the thesis of this post before I did: "we are aware that many clauses in this policy are unenforceable. Our goal is not to catch every violation... our goal is to remove plausible deniability: to force a choice between following the policy and intentionally violating it."

Rust is the proof the ladder is fair. Its policy is prose — Level 0 by trigger — and it says so, out loud, in its own introduction. QGIS threatens reversion and sanctioning from the same rung without the label. Same material, opposite honesty: one wrote "these clauses are unenforceable" where its enforcement should be; the other dressed the conscience test in reversion threats. The difference between them is not strictness. It is whether the policy's own rung is falsifiable.

What a Level 2 policy for AI contributions looks like

Not detection. Process, signed:

  • A provenance trailer on every commit, the same shape as Signed-off-by: Authored-by: human or Authored-by: human, assisted-by: <tool>. No LLM-detection claims — a declaration, required by the CI, refused at the gate when absent. The Linux kernel answer quoted approvingly on HN — "LLM use allowed, but you are fully responsible for the code it produces" — is this rung: responsibility attaching to a signed name instead of to a detection heuristic.
  • Reversion with a logged reason. "Code reversion and sanctioning" already threatened by QGIS becomes enforceable the day reversions carry receipts: which commit, which rule, which reviewer. A sanction that lives in a private conversation is not a control.
  • A published exceptions log. Dawson's "closed door, open case-by-case" (autocomplete replacements, translations) is the right shape — but a case-by-case door with no public log is a door that silently becomes a hallway. The exceptions ledger is the policy's audit trail.
  • Optional, and only if the maintainers want it: canaries for docs. Plant a decoy instruction in the contributing docs and see who commits it — the deliberately-failed probe, already proven useful for grading agents. Cheap, imperfect, honest about being a tripwire rather than a judge.
  • Write the rung into the policy. Rust's LLM policy does it in its own overview — "we are aware that many clauses in this policy are unenforceable" — and that sentence is why nobody can accuse Rust of pretending. A labeled weakness beats an invisible one, in constitutions as much as in code.

None of this detects AI code. Detection is the adversary's game and the adversary is winning it. The receipts regime claims something narrower and true: when a contribution breaks the rules, the break is provable, attributable, and on the record — instead of discoverable, if at all, by vibes.

The cost, stated plainly

The seatbelt tax. A provenance trailer is thirty seconds per commit, forever, on every contributor — including the ninety-nine percent who were never going to game anything. Level 0 costs nothing and catches nothing; Level 2 costs everyone and catches process violations, not authorship. There is no rung with no price. A maintainer who says "my contributors will not accept friction" has chosen Level 0, and after this week's numbers — the pressure is real — that is a defensible choice. It should be a labeled one.

Two honest limits

The survey is a snapshot with disclosed crudeness. Twenty repos chosen by prominence, contributing docs and policy files as the policy surface, workflow names as the enforcement surface — a deep CI-content audit, or a policy living outside those files, would be missed. Five of the six policies are graded from full reads (Rust's was fetched from the Rust Forge; its unenforceable-clauses sentence is quoted from the policy's own overview), one (QGIS) from its merged proposal and the core team's comments. Whether the policy authors would accept my rung assignments is their right to dispute — the rungs are quoted from their own texts so the dispute can be precise.

And QGIS is not wrong to choose survival over verifiability this quarter. Fifty tags and forty closed PRs is a real attempt with real numbers; "unbearable pressure" is not performative. This post argues the stop gap should carry its label — Level 0, honesty-based, revision to follow — the same way this series labels every weakness it confesses, and the same way Rust labels its own clauses. A project that writes its control's rung into the policy has not solved enforcement. It has made the absence of enforcement falsifiable.

Your turn

What does your project's AI policy actually enforce — and at which rung? If you maintain one, link it in the comments with an honest grading: prose, primitive, or gate. And if you have built an enforceable provenance scheme for contributions — trailers, CI gates, canaries, anything that refuses at the host — I want the receipts. The registry only works if the levels travel.

articles.title: I Benchmarked Five JavaScript Data Grids with Up to 800 000 Rows
articles.description: A data grid is where users of an enterprise web app spend most of their day. Support consoles,...
articles.body_html:
A data grid is where users of an enterprise web app spend most of their day. Support consoles, logistics manifests, financial reports: they all come down to a table, and people now expect that table to maintain responsiveness under high workloads. Many JS grid components on the market perform well in a demo with a thousand rows, but what happens when the number of rows increases tens or hundreds of times? That's what really interests developers who need to add the data grid to a modern enterprise-grade app.

Disclosure: I’m a product developer at DHTMLX, so the question isn’t academic for me.

To get an answer worth publishing, I benchmarked five JavaScript Grid components using the same test suite: DHTMLX Grid, AG Grid, Bryntum Grid, DevExtreme DataGrid, and Kendo UI Grid. The benchmark uses the same seeded data, row height, and scroll workload across five dataset sizes (from 10,000 to 800,000 rows). That gives 40 configurations per grid and 200 measurement points across all five grids.

The complete JavaScript Grid performance benchmark repository contains the test suite and configurations needed to reproduce these measurements on your own machine.

What I Measured

I focused on three metrics that cover the main areas where users usually notice performance issues in grid tables.

Building the grid. The time from initializing the grid until the viewport contains the expected number of rows. This measurement ignores grids’ “ready” signals, because each component defines this point differently.

Jump to depth. The time between programmatically jumping to 90% of the dataset and the moment the viewport displays the rows at that position. This shows how quickly grids can catch up when the user decides to move from the beginning of the table to a point close to its end.

Scrolling. A single FPS figure isn't enough, so I collected a series of frame times while the grid’s scroll container was driven programmatically over 50,000 px. Every frame is recorded, allowing us to calculate the median, 95th percentile, and worst frame time. FPS is reported as additional context.

The benchmark uses the same setup for all five grid components: one seeded dataset, a fixed row height of 40 px, and a 1920×1080 viewport. The fixed 40 px row height keeps the scrolling workload comparable across grids. Without it, the same scroll distance could cover a different number of rows in each grid. The rendered height is checked during each run and reports an error if grids do not comply with the 40 px setting.

Now, I want to take a little detour and dwell a bit on frames per second (FPS), the metric everyone publishes, and discuss why it tells surprisingly little about how JS grid components actually behave while scrolling.

Why FPS Numbers Can Be Confusing

The FPS metric reduces an entire sequence of frame times to a single number. That makes it easy to compare at a glance, but it doesn’t show how those frames are distributed.

Let’s say, for instance, that one grid provides mostly smooth frames with occasional long pauses, while another grid may be slower on every frame. These two grid components can have similar FPS numbers, but these are two different behavior patterns. FPS demonstrates how many frames are produced as a whole, but says nothing about consistency or how long the slowest frame takes. As a result, FPS can make occasional stutters and continuous heavy rendering look deceptively similar.

There is another noteworthy factor related to the 60 Hz display used for testing. At this refresh rate, frames that finish within 16.7 ms have the same FPS rate. It means that two grids can show the same FPS, but at the same time, have different frame times.

That is why I took a different approach to scrolling measurement. Instead of relying on FPS, I recorded the frame times themselves and used their distribution to evaluate scrolling performance.

Why FPS Hides Performance Differences: One Example

A single benchmark configuration is enough to show why frame-time distribution provides more information than FPS alone.

The example below uses 100,000 rows, 20 columns, and real HTML content rendered inside cells. It compares the same scrolling scenario using four frame-related metrics: median frame time, 95th percentile (P95), worst observed frame, and the resulting FPS value.

Grid Median frame, ms P95 frame, ms Worst frame, ms FPS
AG Grid 16.7 26.19 69 57
Bryntum 16.6 23.1 38.5 60
DevExtreme 18.7 32.65 72.8 51
DHTMLX 16.6 21.23 41.6 60
Kendo 16.9 95.26 111.5 35

The median stays within a narrow range of 16.6-18.7 ms across all five grids, so it does not show any significant differences in scrolling behavior. The P95 parameter is more revealing: DHTMLX records the lowest value at 21.23 ms, followed by Bryntum at 23.1 ms, AG Grid at 26.19 ms, DevExtreme at 32.65 ms, and Kendo at 95.26. In practical terms, these values mean that 95% of the recorded frames took no more than the corresponding P95 value to render. A lower P95 indicates that a larger share of the scrolling sequence stays within a shorter frame time, while a higher value points to a greater number of slow frames.

The worst-frame values identify the largest single spikes observed during the measurement. Because this metric represents only one frame, it should not be treated as a characteristic of common scrolling performance, but it helps reveal frame-time peaks that median numbers do not show.

The FPS results show the need to consider underlying frame-time data to evaluate scrolling performance properly. DHTMLX and Bryntum both report 60 FPS, followed by AG-Grid with 57 FPS, yet their P95 worst-frame values show more noticeable differences. That is why looking at the full set of frame-time metrics gives a more objective perspective on scrolling performance.

Important Benchmark Details

The benchmark is designed to be transparent and fully reproducible, with the same methodology applied to all five grids. It should help exclude potential biases. A seed drives the row generator, so each testing scenario uses the same generated data. All grid-specific settings added in the benchmark are listed in the project repository. No other performance tuning is applied beyond those documented settings.

Each test is performed five times after one discarded warm-up pass. The browser window remains visible during testing. Each result records the grid version, machine, browser, and display refresh rate used for the run.

All measurements are taken on an eight-core Ryzen 7 4700U.

Here are the exact packages and grid versions used for testing:

Grid npm package Build measured
AG Grid ag-grid-community 36.0.2
Bryntum Grid @​bryntum/grid-trial 7.3.4
DevExtreme DataGrid devextreme 26.1.3
DHTMLX Grid @​dhx/trial-grid 9.3.8
Kendo UI Grid @​progress/kendo-ui 2026.2.520

Note: AG Grid is measured here as the free ag-grid-community package, the other four as commercial trials.

This benchmark focuses on rendering, scrolling, and navigation. Operations like sorting, filtering, and streaming updates are outside the scope because they have many possible implementations and usage patterns, while the benchmark needs to choose one representative workflow to make comparisons meaningful. Instead of horizontal scrolling, the benchmark measures column count as a clearer performance indicator.

How Different Workloads Affect Grid Performance

The benchmark uses four workload variables: row count, column count, cell content, and pinned columns. Each variable is tested independently while the other inputs remain fixed, making it easier to isolate its impact on the measured grid performance.

Row Count

To see how initial rendering changes as the dataset grows, the chart below shows build times with ten columns and rows ranging from 10,000 to 800,000.

Grid 10k 50k 100k 200k 800k
AG Grid 148.6 199.4 255.8 386.1 1149.4
Bryntum 268.6 532.3 838.8 1503.1 5330.2
DevExtreme 180.5 182.8 178.1 179.6 186.1
DHTMLX 55 65.5 73.8 93.3 242.8
Kendo 93.1 93.5 91.1 96.5 115.2

Build time in milliseconds, ten template columns. Bold marks the fastest in each column.

Ranking the values is less useful than putting them on a scale that reflects how people typically perceive delays: sub-100 ms responses generally feel immediate, around 1 second is clearly noticeable, and delays of several seconds can make an application feel unresponsive. Against that scale, DHTMLX remains below 100 ms through 200,000 rows and reaches 242.8 ms at 800,000 rows. Kendo stays close to the 100 ms range across all five sizes, while DevExtreme stays around 180 ms. AG Grid stays below 1 second until the largest dataset, where build time reaches 1149.4 ms. Bryntum crosses the 1-second mark at 200,000 rows and reaches 5330.2 ms at 800,000 rows.

Column Count

The next variable is the number of columns configured in the grid. The chart below shows how P95 frame time changes as the column count increases from 10 to 40, with the dataset fixed at 100,000 rows. The scrolling test remains vertical throughout, so the results measure the rendering cost of a wider grid rather than horizontal scrolling performance.

Grid 10 columns 20 columns 40 columns
AG Grid 18.93 26.19 27.1
Bryntum 19.4 23.1 29.9
DevExtreme 26.34 32.65 30.15
DHTMLX 17.4 21.23 21.07
Kendo 55.6 95.26 173.69

P95 frame time in milliseconds, 100 000 rows. Bold marks the lowest in each column.

DHTMLX records the lowest P95 at all three column counts, with only a small change as the number of columns increases. For four other tested grid components, moving from 10 to 40 columns adds between 3.67 and 10.5 ms to P95. Kendo shows a much larger increase in this configuration, from 55.6 to 173.69 ms, or about 3.1 x times.

Cell Templates

Cell content can also affect scrolling performance, so this test compares the same dataset in two versions: one with rich HTML content such as status pills, star ratings, colored badges, and progress bars, and one with the same fields rendered as plain text. The same markup is generated for each grid, keeping the cell content consistent across the comparison.

The table below shows the result of subtracting plain-text P95 from template P95, in milliseconds, at 100,000 rows. A positive number means that rich content increased P95. A negative number means that the plain-text run was marginally slower.

Grid 10 columns, ms 20 columns, ms 40 columns, ms
AG Grid +1.33 +2.59 +3.51
Bryntum +0.7 +2.1 +7.3
DevExtreme −0.16 +6.43 +3.52
DHTMLX +0.2 +3.6 +3.77
Kendo +7.12 +22.16 +49.89

Template P95 minus plain-text P95, in milliseconds, at 100 000 rows. Differences of about 1 ms in either direction are treated as measurement noise.

For four of the five grids, rich cell content adds only a few milliseconds to P95 in these configurations. Only Kendo shows a much larger increase as the column count grows, reaching 49.89 ms at 40 columns.

The broader takeaway is that rich cell content does not automatically result in a substantial scrolling penalty. In these configurations, the measured overhead is modest for four grids, while Kendo shows a more noticeable sensitivity to richer cell templates.

Pinned Columns

Next, I measure the impact of pinned columns on scrolling performance. For this purpose, the benchmark compares each configuration with three columns pinned against the same configuration with all columns scrolling normally.

P95 with three columns pinned, minus P95 for the same scenario without pinning, in milliseconds:

Grid 10 col @100k, ms 40 col @100k, ms 10 col @800k, ms 40 col @800k, ms
AG Grid +0.67 −0.31 +81.7 +172.56
Bryntum −0.5 +3.2 −0.3 −0.9
DevExtreme +3.36 +6.91 +4.08 +6.52
DHTMLX −0.2 +0.76 −0.1 +1.15
Kendo +1.75 +4.92 +1.3 +7.57

Bold marks the two figures that fall outside measurement noise.

For Bryntum and DHTMLX, adding three pinned columns produces no meaningful increase in P95 in the tested configurations. DevExtreme and Kendo show a small increase, with P95 rising by a few milliseconds. AG Grid is different: the effect is negligible at 100,000 rows but becomes substantial at 800,000 rows, where pinning increases P95 by 81.7 ms with 10 columns and 172.56 ms with 40 columns.

The practical consequence is about testing rather than choosing: a pinned-column layout that measures clean at 100 000 rows is not evidence that it measures clean at 800 000.

Memory Usage

“How much memory does this grid use?” can mean two different things. For page-level budgeting, the relevant figure is the total heap occupied after the grid has been constructed, including the library, dataset, and grid. For comparing the grid instances themselves, the benchmark measures how much additional heap the grid uses after the library and dataset have been loaded.

That is why the benchmark reports both figures. A forced garbage collection is performed before each measurement to remove objects that are no longer in use.

Grid Page total, MB Grid only, MB
AG Grid 320.12 178.78
Bryntum 905.62 761.66
DevExtreme 164.03 13.85
DHTMLX 170.97 30.58
Kendo 162.95 15.14

800 000 rows, 40 template columns. Bold marks the lowest in each column.

The two measurements answer different questions, so a grid that has a lower page total does not necessarily have a lower grid-only memory usage. That is why both results are reported. At 800,000 rows and 40 template columns, page total ranges from 162.95 MB for Kendo to 905.62 MB for Bryntum, while grid-only memory ranges from 13.85 MB for DevExtreme to 761.66 MB for Bryntum. DHTMLX measures 170.97 MB for page total and 30.58 MB for grid-only, keeping memory usage relatively low in both cases.

The difference between Page total and Grid only represents memory that was already present before the grid was constructed, including the loaded library and dataset. Looking at how this difference changes as the number of columns increases gives an additional insight: when moving from 10 to 40 columns, the gap grows by about 1.14–1.15 MB at 10,000 rows and 11.44–11.46 MB at 100,000 rows across all five grids. Because the same dataset is used throughout the benchmark, the matching increase suggests that much of this additional memory comes from the shared data rather than from the grid implementation.

The remaining variation can be used to estimate the library-related part of this memory. Across the tested grids, that estimate ranges from about 2.72 MB to 12.51 MB. These figures represent an inferred memory contribution from the loaded libraries, not their package size on disk.
